chapters.title: Chapter 2: The Gold Standard Era and the Fall of the British Pound

body.text: For roughly four decades before the First World War, most of the world's money was, in effect, a claim on gold, and London, not any gold mine, was where that entire system actually ran from.

markDefs.definition: A monetary system in which a country fixes its currency's value to a specific weight of gold and commits to freely converting that currency into gold on demand at that fixed rate.

children.text: Chapter 1 defined what a reserve currency is and what issuing one is actually worth. This chapter goes back to where the modern story starts: the

era, roughly the 1870s to 1914. It was not the world's first attempt to anchor money to a metal, but it was the first time a genuinely global system of fixed exchange rates connected most of the major trading economies at once, with the British pound sterling sitting at its centre.

markDefs.definition: The classical gold standard's automatic adjustment mechanism: a country running a trade deficit loses gold to pay for it, which shrinks its money supply and lowers domestic prices, making its exports cheaper and imports costlier until the trade balance corrects itself, and vice versa for a surplus country.

children.text: Each participating country fixed its currency to a specific weight of gold and stood ready to convert that currency into gold on demand. Because every currency was pegged to gold, exchange rates between any two gold standard countries were effectively fixed as well, a rupee, a franc, and a mark were all just different labels for a given quantity of gold. The system was meant to be self-correcting through what economists call the

, first described by the economist David Hume well before the era itself. In theory, gold flowed automatically to wherever it was needed to keep trade roughly balanced, no central bank had to actively manage the exchange rate the way modern central banks do.

body.caption: The classical gold standard's core rules

cells: Each currency was defined as a specific weight of gold, set by law and rarely changed
Anyone could exchange paper currency or bank deposits for gold coin at the central bank, and vice versa, without restriction
Trade imbalances were meant to self-correct through gold flows and resulting changes in domestic prices, rather than through deliberate policy
Investors could move capital across borders with little restriction, since currency risk between gold standard countries was minimal

children.text: London and Sterling at the Centre

In practice, the classical gold standard was not a purely mechanical, self-running system. It ran through London. Britain's early industrialisation, its dominant merchant fleet, and the Bank of England's deep and liquid market for short-term credit meant that traders and governments around the world found it easier to hold and settle in sterling-denominated bills of exchange than to physically ship gold bars back and forth. Sterling functioned as a reserve and settlement currency alongside gold itself, decades before the pound formally lost that role to the dollar, the subject of Lesson 2 of this chapter.

children.text: India's Currency Was Pegged to This System Too

markDefs.definition: A monetary arrangement where a country does not hold gold directly as backing for its currency, but instead pegs its currency to another country's gold-backed currency and holds reserves largely in that other currency's assets.

children.text: British India offers a useful, and often overlooked, case study of how the gold standard actually reached beyond Europe. India was on a silver standard through most of the nineteenth century, and when the global price of silver fell sharply relative to gold in the 1870s and 1880s, the silver rupee lost value against gold-backed sterling year after year, straining colonial finances. India's mints were closed to free silver coinage in 1893 to halt the slide, and in 1898 the Fowler Committee formally adopted a

for the rupee, fixed at 1 shilling 4 pence sterling. India never actually needed to hold large stocks of physical gold to back this peg; it held sterling securities in London instead, as its Gold Standard Reserve.

body.title: The Rupee's Path Onto the Gold-Exchange Standard

events.title: The Silver Rupee Established
events.description: The Coinage Act of 1835 set a uniform silver rupee as British India's standard currency.

events.title: The Fall of the Rupee
events.description: A global glut of silver, following new discoveries and several countries demonetising silver, pushed silver's price down against gold. Since the rupee was silver-based and sterling was gold-based, the rupee depreciated steadily against sterling, straining India's gold-denominated obligations to Britain.

events.title: Mints Closed to Free Silver Coinage
events.description: Following the Herschell Committee's recommendation, India's mints stopped freely coining silver rupees, a step toward breaking the rupee's automatic link to the falling price of silver.

events.title: The Fowler Committee's Gold-Exchange Standard
events.description: The rupee was formally fixed at 1 shilling 4 pence sterling, backed by a Gold Standard Reserve held mainly in sterling securities in London rather than physical gold in India.

events.title: The System Suspended
events.description: Like the rest of the classical gold standard, the arrangement was disrupted by the outbreak of the First World War, the subject this lesson turns to next.

body.text: Notice what the rupee's Gold Standard Reserve actually was: sterling assets sitting in London, not gold sitting in Bombay or Calcutta. India's monetary stability was, in effect, backed by trust in another country's currency rather than trust in a physical metal it held itself. That is a gold-exchange standard, not a pure gold standard, and it is a direct historical preview of exactly the kind of dollar dependency this course examines in Chapter 1 and returns to for the rupee specifically in Chapter 4.

children.text: The classical gold standard delivered genuinely low inflation and predictable exchange rates for four decades, which is why some commentators still romanticise it. But the same rigidity that made it stable also made it unforgiving. Because the money supply was tied to gold reserves, a country could not simply create more money to fight a recession or rising unemployment without risking its gold peg; contemporaries called sticking to this discipline playing by the rules of the game, and it frequently meant sacrificing domestic economic conditions to defend the exchange rate. Gold supply itself grew unevenly, tied to the pace of new mining discoveries rather than the needs of a growing global economy, which built a persistent deflationary bias into the system. And for colonies like India, the peg was set and managed from London, not Delhi, with India's own monetary interests distinctly secondary to Britain's.

body.title: The Classical Gold Standard: Benefits vs Limits

columns.label: Benefits
points: Stable, predictable exchange rates across most major trading economies
Generally low and stable inflation over the long run
Low currency risk encouraged large-scale cross-border trade and investment
A single, globally recognised store of value in gold

columns.label: Limits
points: Money supply growth was constrained by gold discoveries, not economic needs, creating a deflationary bias
Central banks often had to sacrifice domestic employment and growth to defend the gold peg
The system depended heavily on London and the Bank of England, not a neutral automatic mechanism
Colonial economies like India had their monetary policy set to serve the coloniser's interests first

body.title: Explain the Rupee's 1893 Decision
body.scenario: By the early 1890s, India's government faced a growing problem: it owed fixed, gold-denominated payments to Britain, known as home charges, for administrative and military costs, but its revenues were collected in a silver rupee that kept losing value against gold. Each year, more rupees were needed to cover the same gold-denominated bill.
body.prompt: Based on what this lesson covered about the price-specie-flow mechanism and the shift to a gold-exchange standard, why would closing the mints to free silver coinage in 1893, followed by fixing the rupee to sterling in 1898, have addressed this specific problem?
body.modelAnswer: As long as the rupee's value was determined by the open-market price of silver, it kept falling every time silver's global price fell, directly worsening the gap between India's silver-denominated revenues and its gold-denominated obligations to Britain. Closing the mints to free coinage broke the rupee's automatic link to the silver market, letting the government control the rupee's supply and effectively manage its value rather than leaving it to silver prices. Fixing the rupee to sterling in 1898 went a step further, tying its value to the currency the home charges were actually owed in, so the exchange rate that mattered most for the government's own finances was finally fixed rather than sliding every year.

body.title: Before You Move to Lesson 2
steps: Write down, in your own words, the difference between a gold standard and a gold-exchange standard
Note the year the classical gold standard broke down, and think about what a major war would do to a system built on free cross-border convertibility
Recall from Chapter 1 what full convertibility and network effects mean for reserve currency status, and consider how sterling already had both by 1913
Move to Lesson 2, which covers how two world wars ended sterling's dominance and set up the dollar's rise

body.title: Check Your Understanding
body.question: What best describes the gold-exchange standard the Indian rupee was placed on in 1898?
options: India held large reserves of physical gold domestically to back the rupee
The rupee was fixed to sterling and backed mainly by sterling securities held in London, rather than physical gold in India
India abandoned any fixed exchange rate and let the rupee float freely against silver
The rupee was pegged directly to the US dollar instead of the British pound
body.explanation: Under the 1898 arrangement recommended by the Fowler Committee, the rupee was fixed at 1 shilling 4 pence sterling, with India's Gold Standard Reserve held mainly as sterling securities in London rather than physical gold within India itself, a defining feature of a gold-exchange standard as opposed to a pure gold standard.

body.text: Dates, exchange rate figures, and statistics on sterling's share of world trade finance and Britain's foreign investment stock in this lesson are presented as widely cited historical approximations for teaching purposes, and different economic historians report slightly different estimates depending on methodology. This lesson is educational content on monetary history, not investment advice.

points: The classical gold standard, roughly 1870s to 1914, fixed major currencies to gold and to each other, with adjustment meant to happen automatically through gold flows and price changes
In practice the system ran through London and sterling, which functioned as a reserve and settlement currency alongside gold itself, financing an estimated 60% of world trade by 1913
British India's rupee moved from a silver standard to a gold-exchange standard in 1898, pegged to sterling and backed mainly by sterling securities held in London rather than gold held in India

The system's rigidity was also its weakness: gold supply constrained money creation, central banks often sacrificed domestic conditions to defend the peg, and colonial economies had their monetary policy set abroad
This sets up Lesson 2: two world wars and the strain of financing them broke the classical gold standard for good and began sterling's long decline as the world's reserve currency
